strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in visual multi-task learning: improving generalization while retaining a shared model. Separately aggregating task-loss and sharpness-related gradients is a concrete, modular design compatible with several existing optimizers.

Tables 1–4 show consistent aggregate improvements over MGDA, PCGrad, CAGrad, and IMTL across classification and dense prediction benchmarks. For example, F-CAGrad improves MultiMNIST average accuracy from 95.01% to 95.95% and reduces CelebA average error from 8.52% to 8.22%.

The supplementary calibration results add value beyond accuracy. On MultiFashion, average Brier score improves from 0.246 to 0.179 and ECE from 0.117 to 0.033. Perturbation experiments and sharpness measurements provide additional evidence consistent with the regularization hypothesis.

Figure 1 and Algorithm 1 make the proposed procedure understandable. The manuscript credits the underlying SAM, ASAM, gradient aggregation methods, and datasets, and supplies useful architecture and training details.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated experimentally. Section 5.3 primarily provides diagnostics rather than component ablations. Missing comparisons include SAM/ASAM applied to a scalarized multi-task loss and direct aggregation of per-task SAM gradients without the proposed decomposition. Consequently, the results establish benefits over conventional training but do not establish why this particular multi-task construction is needed.

The generalization theorem has substantive gaps as stated. The vector maximum in Equation (4) is interpreted as a common worst-case shared perturbation, although different tasks can have incompatible maximizers. A componentwise supremum would support a different interpretation. Furthermore, Appendix A bounds Gaussian-tail loss contributions using an unstated bounded-loss assumption; applicability to the experimental losses is not established.

The connection between the bound and Algorithm 1 remains incomplete. The bound considers simultaneous shared and task-specific perturbations, whereas the algorithm evaluates them separately, omitting their interaction. Separately aggregating loss and flatness gradients and then adding the results also does not generally preserve descent for every task or both criteria. Equation (5) motivates a surrogate but does not establish the claimed simultaneous improvement.

The practical cost is inadequately evaluated. Algorithm 1 adds perturbed gradient evaluations for each task, potentially making the overhead substantial for the 40-task CelebA experiment. No runtime, memory, or matched-compute comparison is reported, leaving the accuracy–training-cost tradeoff unclear.

Important reproducibility details remain unresolved. Appendix B.2 states that experiments use ASAM, while the main equations and pseudocode describe Euclidean SAM; the corresponding adaptive update is not specified. Selected perturbation radii and their validation procedure are also missing. The claimed public implementation has no repository link in the supplied manuscript, and Tables 2–4 omit variability estimates, limiting assessment of smaller improvements.
